implementation_notes: CompletableFuture is the stdlib realization: supplyAsync/runAsync start the work and return immediately, and whenComplete/thenAccept/exceptionally register the callbacks that run when the stage completes - on the completing thread, or on the caller if it is already complete. The CompletionStage chain replaces the hand-rolled event object, while orTimeout/completeOnTimeout cover deadlines; prefer it for non-UI work where composition matters, and remember that the underlying task is not interrupted by CompletableFuture.cancel.
pitfalls: Callbacks run on the completing thread (a pool thread or whoever finished the stage): touching Swing/JavaFX state there without SwingUtilities.invokeLater/Platform.runLater violates the toolkit's thread rule.
Blocking inside a callback (join()/get()) can deadlock once the common pool has no free thread, and CompletableFuture.cancel does not interrupt the underlying task.
An exception thrown inside a callback is captured in the returned stage; ignoring that stage loses the failure.

variants.name: SwingWorker on the Event Dispatch Thread
variants.idiom_name: SwingWorker<T,V>: doInBackground + done/publish/process on the EDT
variants.implementation_notes: The classic UI realization: execute() starts doInBackground on a worker thread and returns at once; done() and process() run on the Event Dispatch Thread, so completion and interim results reach Swing safely, get() exposes the result and throws for failures, and cancel(true) plus isCancelled() implement advisory cancellation. Choose it when the caller is Swing and the operation is one-shot; for non-UI work prefer CompletableFuture, and note SwingWorker is single-use.
pitfalls: done()/process() run on the EDT: long work there re-freezes the UI, and touching UI state from doInBackground is illegal.
publish() is coalesced, so process() can receive several interim results at once, and get() inside done() throws ExecutionException/CancellationException that must be handled.
SwingWorker is single-use: calling execute() a second time throws IllegalStateException, so it cannot serve as a reusable event source.

variants.name: Flow Publisher/Subscriber callbacks (onNext/onError/onComplete)
variants.idiom_name: java.util.concurrent.Flow Publisher/Subscriber with a terminal onComplete
variants.implementation_notes: Java's standard reactive-streams interop models an event stream: a Publisher hands the Subscriber a Subscription, calls onNext for each element or progress update and exactly one terminal onComplete or onError, so multi-event completion plus backpressure arrive through one callback interface. Choose it when several events must reach a subscriber under demand control; it is heavier than CompletableFuture for a single result.
pitfalls: onNext/onError/onComplete follow the subscription's demand and the implementation's threading rules: a subscriber that blocks in onNext stalls the publisher, and items must never be delivered without a request.
onComplete and onError are mutually exclusive and terminal: continuing to request items afterwards, or treating onComplete as an interim signal, breaks the protocol.
